Online retail satisfaction: 26 years without real progress

In twenty-six years, online retail has changed everything: next-day delivery, one-click payment, free returns, personalized recommendations. Yet the satisfaction of its customers has barely moved.

According to the American Customer Satisfaction Index (ACSI), the US online retail satisfaction score was 78 out of 100 in 2000. In 2026, it stands at 79. In between, it moved within a narrow range, from 77 to 84 points.

An almost flat curve

The best score of the period came in 2003, at 84 points. The lowest points, 77, were recorded in 2001 and again in 2021. The rest of the time, the index moves between 78 and 83, with no lasting upward trend.

Recent years confirm that stability: 80 points from 2022 to 2024, then 79 in 2025 and 2026. In other words, despite massive investment in logistics, interfaces and personalization, the experience customers perceive is no longer really improving.

Some caution is needed: a national index aggregates millions of very different experiences. But the lack of progress over such a long period is worth a closer look.

Why expectations move at the same pace

One plausible explanation is expectations. Every improvement quickly becomes the new norm. Two-day delivery was a selling point in 2010; today it is considered standard. What delighted customers yesterday merely meets expectations tomorrow.

In that context, a stable score does not mean nothing was done. It means retailers' efforts were absorbed by rising demands. To move forward, doing better in general is no longer enough; you need to understand precisely what still disappoints customers.

Competition also plays a role. Online shoppers compare every retailer with the best one they know. A smooth experience at one store raises the bar for all the others, which keeps the average score from climbing even when most retailers improve.

A score says how much. Words say why

That is the limit of any overall indicator: it measures a level, not a cause. A score of 79 out of 100 does not say whether customers complain about delivery times, return fees, product quality or how hard it is to reach customer service.

Those answers are in what customers write and say: product reviews, post-delivery comments, tickets, emails, calls. Each message explains part of the score. Taken together, they draw a precise map of pain points.

Our analysis of 200 G2 reviews showed how an average rating can hide frustrations heavily concentrated on one topic.

Public data cannot settle which explanation is right. That is exactly why every company benefits from looking at its own customer feedback, which holds the answer for its specific situation, rather than reasoning on a national average.

Read all the feedback, not a sample

Volume is the main obstacle. A mid-sized online retailer receives thousands of reviews and messages every month. Reading them all by hand is impossible, and a sample of a few dozen gives a misleading picture.

Automatic language analysis can process all of this feedback: grouping topics, measuring the emotions attached to them, tracking changes week after week. It brings out the pain points that really weigh on satisfaction, and the ones that are starting to emerge.

The models used are Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case; data stays hosted in France.

Weekly tracking also catches seasonal effects, such as holiday delivery peaks, before they leave a lasting mark on reviews.

From index to action

A national index like the ACSI is a benchmark. At company level, the goal is different: knowing what to fix first. That means linking the satisfaction score to the reasons customers give, then tracking the effect of fixes over time.

Retailers that do this regularly can break out of the plateau. Not by promising more, but by removing, one by one, the pain points their customers already describe. Our retail and e-commerce page gives concrete examples.

A simple method is to pick the two or three most cited pain points each quarter, fix them, then check in the following feedback whether they decline. This short cycle produces visible progress, where an overall index takes years to move.

It also highlights what already works: the things customers mention positively without being asked are the ones to protect during the next changes.

What this means for you

A satisfaction score that has been flat for 26 years will not move with one more indicator. custovox.ai reads your reviews, tickets and calls to identify the pain points that really weigh on your customers' satisfaction, and to track the effect of your fixes.
